items.question: Describe the legal status of DSC acknowledgements and why they must be handled correctly.
items.good: A DSC acknowledgement legally confirms receipt of an alert and, for a distress alert, indicates that the acknowledging station is taking control of the SAR response. In Sea Area A1 acknowledgements should be sent by the coast station, not by other ships, to avoid duplicated acknowledgements interfering with SAR coordination. Ships should only acknowledge if no coast station has done so and after allowing time for that to happen; the acknowledgement must then be followed up on voice on Channel 16.

items.question: Describe how DSC channel allocations differ from voice channels on VHF.
items.good: DSC uses a single dedicated data channel, Channel 70, on 156.525 MHz for all its digital selective calls — distress, urgency, safety and routine categories alike. Voice traffic then follows on a separate voice channel, most commonly Channel 16 for distress/urgency/safety and a designated working channel for routine. This separation ensures that DSC signalling cannot corrupt live voice traffic and vice versa.

items.question: Explain how good radio discipline contributes to overall safety at sea.
items.good: Good radio discipline keeps Channel 16 and DSC clear for distress and urgency traffic, minimises misunderstandings between commercial and pleasure craft, and ensures that SAR alerts are heard, coordinated and acted upon quickly. It also reflects a general standard of seamanship — a well-disciplined operator is usually a well-prepared skipper. Discipline directly saves lives.

items.question: Explain the purpose of Digital Selective Calling in the GMDSS system.
items.good: DSC provides an automated digital layer on top of VHF (and MF/HF) radio, so that distress, urgency, safety and routine calls can be addressed to specific stations, groups or all stations without operator intervention on the receiving end. It replaces continuous manual watchkeeping on voice frequencies with automated watch on Channel 70, guarantees delivery of key data (MMSI, position, category) and switches the receiver to a voice channel for follow-up. It is the alerting backbone of GMDSS.

items.question: Explain why marinas and yacht clubs often publish their preferred working channels.
items.good: Publishing a preferred working channel means visiting skippers know exactly where to call for berthing, fuel or race information without cluttering Channel 16 or trial-and-error. It also lets the marina staff monitor a single, agreed channel throughout the day. Typical published channels include Channel 80 for UK marinas, Channel 9 for many US marinas, or a locally assigned working channel.

items.question: Describe the concept of national "small craft safety" channels and give one example of their intended use.
items.good: Some administrations designate national small craft or leisure safety channels to keep pleasure-boat traffic off congested main channels. For example, in the UK Channel 8 is used for intership traffic between leisure vessels and Channel 67 was historically the small craft safety channel for the UK Coastguard, used for non-distress safety communications between leisure vessels and HM Coastguard. Their aim is to keep Channel 16 free while still serving small craft needs.

items.question: Describe a situation where two vessels might need to agree on an alternative working channel due to congestion.

The initiating station proposes an alternative such as Ch 77 or Ch 8; the other confirms. Both then switch, listen briefly to ensure the alternative is clear, and continue the conversation. This preserves an orderly channel plan without blocking others.

items.question: Explain the importance of monitoring channel 16 (and/or a designated DSC watch channel) while at sea.
items.good: Channel 16 is the international voice distress, urgency, safety and calling channel; the DSC watch on Channel 70 provides automated distress alerting. Continuous watch on both is required so the vessel can hear MAYDAY, MAYDAY RELAY, urgency and safety calls, respond to SAR requests, and be called by other vessels or the coastguard. Missing a distress call because of poor watchkeeping is a serious lapse of duty.

items.good: Channel 70 (156.525 MHz) carries only the short digital DSC signalling — the alert. Once the DSC call is received, the operator (or the radio itself) switches to the associated voice channel to conduct the actual conversation: Ch 16 for distress/urgency/safety, or a working channel for routine. DSC and voice thus form a two-step process: signalling on Ch 70, conversation on the voice channel.

items.question: Explain the concept of "interference" in the legal context of radio communications and give two examples.
items.good: Interference is any emission, radiation or induction that degrades, obstructs or interrupts an authorised radio service. In marine VHF terms, examples include keeping the PTT depressed on Channel 16, which blocks other users from calling for distress, and using non type-approved equipment that transmits outside the allocated channel bandwidth and bleeds into adjacent channels. Interference — whether accidental or wilful — is prohibited under the ITU Radio Regulations and national law.

items.question: Explain why a calling channel is used and why you must then shift to a working channel.
items.good: A calling channel — Channel 16 or, in some areas, Channel 9 — is monitored by many stations, so it is where initial contact is most likely to be heard. Once the two stations have established contact they must shift promptly to a working channel because a long conversation on the calling channel would block distress calls and monopolise a shared resource. The calling channel therefore acts as a doorway; the actual conversation happens elsewhere.

items.question: Explain why it is dangerous to use emergency channels for routine traffic.
items.good: Emergency channels — Channel 16 for voice and Channel 70 for DSC — are the primary means by which a MAYDAY reaches ships and shore stations. Routine traffic on these channels masks distress calls, wastes seconds that a rescue may depend on, and undermines the discipline expected on the channel. It also breaches the Radio Regulations and can result in fines or revocation of the operator certificate.

items.question: Describe the function of the volume control and how it should be set during watchkeeping.
items.good: The volume control sets the audio output level to the loudspeaker (and any external speaker). During watchkeeping it must be high enough that Channel 16 and DSC alerts are clearly audible above engine, wind and background noise, but not so loud that it distorts or masks other cockpit conversation. Before watch, adjust volume against the receiver's background noise (with squelch open) and then re-set squelch.

items.question: Explain when a vessel may cease continuous listening watch under the regulations.
items.good: Continuous listening watch on Channel 16 and DSC may be ceased when the vessel is in port with the radio powered down and moored, when the operator has been released from watch by the appropriate control station (e.g. after entering a VTS area where watch is transferred to the local channel), or in a designated harbour where local rules replace the Channel 16 watch. On leisure vessels the watch may be relaxed while the vessel is out of the water or in secure berth.

items.question: Explain why passengers and unqualified crew should not operate the VHF radio in normal circumstances.

National law requires a certificated operator (SRC or higher). Unqualified persons should therefore only use the radio in a genuine distress when no certificated operator is available — in which case they may transmit a MAYDAY under the master's authority.

items.question: Explain how Maritime Rescue Coordination Centres (MRCCs) interact with ships via VHF and DSC.

They authenticate the alert, gather the nature of distress, position, number of persons on board and injuries, task SAR units and nearby vessels, and control on-scene traffic — often imposing SEELONCE MAYDAY. All communication is logged. In the UK MRCCs are run by HM Coastguard.

They exchange short SMCP-based passing arrangements — for example "I intend to overtake you on your starboard side" — communicate with VTS about traffic movements, and often with pilots or tugs on dedicated channels. Discipline is high because a misheard instruction between two large ships can lead to a collision.

Discipline in channel choice therefore directly protects the safety function of VHF.

Keeping the radio powered and set to Ch 16 (plus DSC watch on Ch 70) is a core watchkeeping requirement whenever underway.

Speak at a normal conversational level about 5 cm from the mic; the radio's audio circuitry does the amplification.

items.question: Distinguish between SOLAS and non-SOLAS vessels and explain how this affects VHF/SRC certification requirements.
items.good: SOLAS vessels are commercial ships of 300 GT or more on international voyages and all passenger ships subject to the SOLAS Convention; they must comply with mandatory GMDSS equipment and operator certification (GOC or ROC). In short, SOLAS = mandatory full GMDSS + higher certificates; non-SOLAS + VHF = SRC minimum.

items.question: Under what circumstances is a vessel master legally obliged to respond to a distress call?

The obligation applies equally to commercial and leisure vessels.

items.question: Define "procedure words" (pro-words) in radio communications.
items.good: Procedure words (pro-words) are short standardised words or phrases used to control the flow of a radio conversation and to convey specific meanings unambiguously — for example OVER, OUT, ROGER, WILCO, SAY AGAIN, CORRECTION, I SPELL, THIS IS. items.question: Demonstrate correct use of the handheld microphone, including distance and speaking angle.

Ships should only acknowledge if no coast station has done so and after allowing time for that to happen; the acknowledgement must then be followed up on voice on Channel 16.

items.question: Explain and demonstrate the limitations of range when using the handheld from different points on the vessel.
items.good: Handheld range is limited by antenna height and body absorption. From the cockpit at deck level (~1 m) expect 3–5 nm to another handheld; from the mast steps (~5 m) up to 8–10 nm; below decks the range drops sharply. Position the operator with a clear view towards the intended recipient, keep the antenna vertical, and hold the handheld away from body and metal structures. Do not rely on a handheld for offshore distress alerting.

items.question: Describe three typical situations where a PAN PAN call would be appropriate.
items.good: Typical PAN PAN situations include: (1) a person on board with a serious medical condition (broken limb, chest pain) not yet life-threatening; (2) engine failure in a busy or hazardous area but no immediate risk of sinking; (3) loss of steering in open water. items.good: After the announcement on Ch 16, once the coast station is on its working channel, use the standard construct: "(coast station name), THIS IS (vessel name), REQUEST YOU REPEAT SAFETY BROADCAST, OVER" or specify: "REQUEST YOU SAY AGAIN ALL AFTER (word), OVER." Do not attempt to reply directly to the casualty in a language you cannot handle. English is the international working language and MRCC will bridge any language gap.

items.question: Explain how the ITU Radio Regulations classify distress, urgency, and safety signals.

items.good: OUT means "this transmission is finished and no reply is expected — I am terminating the conversation." It is used to close a call, whereas OVER hands over for a reply. Combining them as "OVER AND OUT" is meaningless and incorrect: either you expect a reply (OVER) or you do not (OUT).
